scams.name: Philadelphia Airport (PHL) Taxi & Rideshare Overcharges
scams.description:
Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) is 12 km from Center City. The legitimate licensed taxi fare to Center City is a $28.50 flat rate (the official PHL Taxi Zone rate, no meter needed — it is published at the taxi stand). Uber and Lyft operate from the Zone 2 pickup with app-regulated fares running $25–$45 depending on surge. The scam comes in a few variants: (1) drivers soliciting inside baggage claim or just outside the doors offer a "flat $50" to Center City — unlicensed, and rejecting the posted $28.50 rate; (2) Uber and Lyft drivers accept the ride, then insist on cash "tips" or add-on fees at dropoff; (3) "limo" or "black car" touts quote $75–$100 "fixed" for what should be $28.50. Travelers consistently emphasize the same rule at PHL: don't take rides from anyone soliciting inside the terminal. The flat rate to Center City is a PHL regulation, so any driver claiming "no flat rate" or "meter only" for a Center City trip is running the scam.

For older travelers arriving at PHL, here is the practical playbook: (1) take the licensed taxi queue outside Zone 5 and confirm "$28.50 flat rate to Center City" before boarding; (2) use Uber or Lyft at the official Zone 2 pickup, and screenshot the fare estimate; (3) the SEPTA Airport Line train runs every 30 minutes to Jefferson Station for $6.75 — scam-proof; (4) never engage drivers approaching inside the terminal or at baggage claim; (5) keep a photo of the PHL taxi rate card on your phone for reference.
scams.avoidance: Take a licensed taxi from Zone 5 outside baggage claim and confirm the $28.50 Center City flat rate. Use Uber or Lyft from the Zone 2 pickup, and screenshot the fare estimate before boarding. Take the SEPTA Airport Line train to Jefferson Station: $6.75, every 30 minutes. Never engage drivers soliciting inside the terminal. Keep a photo of the PHL taxi rate card on your phone for reference.
scams.location: Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) arrivals, ground transportation pickup zones, Zone 2 rideshare area
scams.tldr: PHL is 12 km from Center City, and the official licensed taxi fare is a published $28.50 flat rate — no meter needed. Drivers soliciting inside the terminal offer "flat $50," rideshare drivers demand cash "tips" at dropoff, and "black car" touts quote $75–$100 for a trip that should cost $28.50.

scams.name: Liberty Bell & Independence Hall 'Skip-the-Line' Ticket Scam
scams.description:
The Liberty Bell Center is free to enter — no ticket required. Independence Hall requires a timed-entry ticket during peak season (March–December), and these are free when obtained through the National Park Service (nps.gov/inde or recreation.gov) with a small $1 reservation fee. The scam comes in a few variants: (1) third-party reseller websites sell "skip-the-line Independence Hall tickets" for $20–$60 per person — charging for tickets that are free; (2) street touts near 5th and Chestnut or the Visitor Center sell "priority tour" packages at $30 and up; (3) "Liberty Bell VIP experience" bundles run $80 and up per person, though the Liberty Bell has no VIP tier — it is a walk-in, free museum. The scam relies on tourists not realizing the sites are operated by the National Park Service and charge nothing beyond the $1 reservation fee. Third-party resellers sometimes show up in Google ads for "Liberty Bell tickets," so scroll past the sponsored results to reach the official NPS website.

For older travelers visiting Independence Hall, here is the clean route: (1) book a timed-entry ticket at recreation.gov or the NPS website (nps.gov/inde) for $1 per person, March–December; (2) in January and February no ticket is needed — walk-in admission; (3) the Liberty Bell Center is always free, with no ticket and no reservation needed; (4) the ranger-led tour of Independence Hall — the Assembly Room where the Declaration and Constitution were signed — is the highlight, so don't skip it; (5) reject all third-party "skip-the-line" websites and street touts offering tickets above $2.
scams.avoidance: Book Independence Hall timed entry at recreation.gov or nps.gov/inde: $1 per person. In January and February, no ticket is needed — just walk in. The Liberty Bell Center is always free, with no ticket and no reservation. Reject all "skip-the-line" Liberty Bell offers — the Bell has no line ticketing. If tickets show "sold out" on the NPS site, wait for the same-day release at the Independence Visitor Center.
scams.location: Independence National Historical Park (Independence Hall, Liberty Bell Center), Market Street approach, online reseller sites
scams.tldr: The Liberty Bell Center is free, and Independence Hall is a free, timed-entry ticket through the National Park Service with only a $1 reservation fee. Reseller websites and street touts sell these free tickets for $20–$60, and bogus "Liberty Bell VIP experience" bundles run $80 and up for a walk-in museum.

scams.name: Reading Terminal Market & South Street Tourist-Menu Overcharge
scams.description:
Philadelphia's signature foods — cheesesteaks, soft pretzels, Italian roast pork — carry major resident-to-tourist pricing gaps. Reading Terminal Market itself is generally fair-priced and a genuine Philly institution, but some tourist-facing stalls, particularly near the 12th and Arch entrance, charge $18 and up for cheesesteaks that cost $10–$13 at authentic South Philly venues. South Street has become a tourist strip where laminated-photo-menu venues charge $20–$25 for subpar cheesesteaks. The famous "Pat's vs. Geno's" at 9th and Passyunk is itself now a tourist tradition — locals debate endlessly whether either is worth the hype — and both charge $15–$16 per cheesesteak, which is acceptable for the experience. But if you want a genuinely great cheesesteak at residential pricing, the names locals point to are different: Jim's South Street (closed after a fire but rebuilding), John's Roast Pork (Snyder Ave, $12–$14), Dalessandro's (Henry Ave, Roxborough, $10–$12), and Angelo's Pizzeria (9th and Fitzwater, $13).

For older travelers, here is the practical guide: (1) Reading Terminal Market is the safest one-stop Philly food experience, with posted prices and quality vendors such as DiNic's roast pork ($12–$14), Beiler's donuts, and Tommy DiNic's; (2) avoid South Street cheesesteak venues entirely — they are always tourist-priced and lower quality; (3) Pat's vs. Geno's is experience-tourism, not value-tourism, so go if you want the photo and skip it if you want the food; (4) John's Roast Pork (Snyder Ave) is widely considered the best cheesesteak in Philly and is residentially priced; (5) always ask for "wit" (with onions) or "witout" — the lingo matters.
scams.avoidance: At Reading Terminal Market, try DiNic's roast pork ($12–$14), Tommy DiNic's, and Beiler's — all with posted prices. For cheesesteaks, go to John's Roast Pork ($12–$14), Dalessandro's ($10–$12), or Angelo's Pizzeria ($13). Pat's vs. Geno's ($15–$16) is experience-tourism only, not value. Avoid South Street cheesesteak venues — all tourist-priced. Learn "wit" or "witout" (with or without onions) for the authentic order.
scams.location: Reading Terminal Market (12th & Arch), South Street tourist strip, cheesesteak venues near Independence Mall
scams.tldr: Philly's signature foods carry big resident-to-tourist pricing gaps. Tourist-facing stalls near Reading Terminal Market's 12th and Arch entrance charge $18 and up for cheesesteaks that cost $10–$13 in South Philly, and South Street's laminated-menu venues charge $20–$25 for subpar versions.

scams.name: Philadelphia Art Museum 'Rocky Steps' Tour Touts
scams.description:
The Philadelphia Museum of Art's 72-step east entrance — famous as the "Rocky Steps" from the 1976 film — is a free photo destination. The museum itself charges $30 for adult admission, with "pay what you wish" on the first Sunday of the month and on Friday evenings from 5:00 to 8:45 PM. The scam comes in a few variants: (1) street touts near the bronze Rocky statue at the bottom of the steps offer a "professional photo" at $20–$50 per shot, then demand $200 and up for a "photo release"; (2) "Rocky-themed walking tours" are marketed at $60–$90 per person for what is essentially a 10-minute walk up free public stairs; (3) "skip-the-line museum tickets" sell for $60 per person when the museum has no line.

For older travelers, here is the practical playbook: (1) the Rocky Steps are free — walk up at your own pace and take your own photos; (2) the Rocky statue at the base of the steps is a popular photo spot, so bring your own camera, wait your turn, and ignore the touts; (3) museum admission is $30 for adults through the official philamuseum.org or at the door; (4) the "pay what you wish" first Sunday and Friday evenings are legitimate Philadelphia Museum of Art programs; (5) skip the "Rocky walking tours" — the entire experience is 15 minutes on your own time, for free.
scams.avoidance: The Rocky Steps are free — walk up at your own pace. Bring your own camera or phone for Rocky statue photos. Museum admission is $30 for adults through philamuseum.org or at the door. "Pay what you wish" is offered the first Sunday and Friday evenings from 5:00 to 8:45 PM. Skip all "Rocky walking tours" — it's a 15-minute free experience.
scams.location: Philadelphia Museum of Art (the 'Rocky Steps'), Logan Circle area, Benjamin Franklin Parkway approach
scams.tldr: The Philadelphia Museum of Art's "Rocky Steps" and the bronze Rocky statue are free to visit. Touts offer a "professional photo" for $20–$50, then demand $200 and up for a "photo release," sell "Rocky walking tours" at $60–$90 for a 10-minute climb, and hawk "skip-the-line" tickets for a museum that has no line.

scams.name: Center City Pickpockets & Street Scams
scams.description:
Philadelphia has moderate opportunistic pickpocket activity concentrated at tourist choke points: SEPTA subway platforms (15th Street, City Hall, 8th and Market), Market East during tourist shopping hours, Rittenhouse Square on summer weekends, and the Independence Mall area during peak season. The patterns are typical of major US cities — not organized-crime-scale like Barcelona, but persistent enough to warrant a defensive posture. The related street scams come in a few variants: (1) someone approaches at Market East with an "I need $40 for bus fare home" story; (2) a "cup game" or three-card monte appears occasionally in the Love Park tourist areas (it's illegal, and everyone playing is a shill); (3) fake panhandlers with well-rehearsed scripts target tourists specifically near Independence Mall; (4) "AirPods for sale" street vendors at SEPTA stations sell counterfeit electronics.

For older travelers, here is the defensive playbook: (1) wear a crossbody bag zipped in front during any SEPTA subway ride, Center City walk, or tourist-site queue; (2) keep your phone in a zipped inner pocket, not a back pocket or an outer backpack; (3) carry only what you need — $60 in cash plus one card and ID in a front pocket, with your passport and backup in the hotel safe; (4) ignore street-scam approaches (bus fare, emergency money, the cup game) — all are scams; (5) SEPTA subways are safe during daytime hours but less so after 10 PM, so use Uber or Lyft for a late-night return.
scams.avoidance: Wear a crossbody bag zipped in front during any SEPTA ride or Center City walk. Keep your phone in a zipped inner pocket, never a back pocket or outer backpack. Carry only $60 in cash plus one card and ID; keep your passport and backup in the hotel safe. Ignore street-scam approaches (bus fare, cup game, AirPods, emergencies). Use Uber or Lyft for a late-night Center City return rather than SEPTA after 10 PM.
scams.location: Center City pedestrian zones, SEPTA subway stations (particularly 15th Street/City Hall), Rittenhouse Square tourist crowds, Market East
scams.tldr: Opportunistic pickpocketing clusters at tourist choke points — SEPTA platforms at 15th Street, City Hall, and 8th and Market, plus Market East, Rittenhouse Square, and Independence Mall. Street scams include "bus fare home" approaches, three-card monte at Love Park, and counterfeit "AirPods" sold at SEPTA stations.

scams.name: Philadelphia Airbnb & Short-Term Rental Fraud
scams.description:
Philadelphia has a well-documented short-term-rental fraud pattern targeting tourists visiting for summer events, the Broad Street Run, or historical sightseeing. The scam works like this: a listing on Airbnb or Facebook Marketplace advertises a Center City or Old City apartment at 25–40% below comparable hotel rates; the "host" asks for a deposit via Zelle or Venmo before confirming the booking; and the listing is either fraudulent (the apartment doesn't exist) or the "host" cancels the Airbnb reservation and keeps the off-platform deposit. In a related variant, hosts request a scan of your ID and a photo of your credit card "for verification" through messaging, then use your information for identity theft. In another, a "local agent" claims to manage multiple Airbnbs and offers a "free upgrade" if you book off-platform and direct.

For older travelers considering an Airbnb or short-term rental in Philadelphia, here is the protective playbook: (1) book only through Airbnb or VRBO, with platform-verified payment and cancellation protection; (2) refuse Zelle, Venmo, or bank-transfer payment requests from any "host"; (3) refuse off-platform ID-scan requests — Airbnb handles ID verification on-platform; (4) verify listings with at least 20 reviews from the last 12 months; (5) for a safer alternative, choose a major licensed hotel with posted prices: The Ritz-Carlton Philadelphia, Four Seasons, Kimpton Hotel Palomar, Loews Philadelphia, or Hyatt Centric Center City — all bookable through Booking.com or the hotel's own site.
scams.avoidance: Book only through Airbnb or VRBO with platform-verified payment. Refuse Zelle, Venmo, or bank transfers from "hosts." Refuse off-platform ID-scan requests. Verify listings with 20 or more reviews from the last 12 months. Licensed hotels: Ritz-Carlton, Four Seasons, Kimpton, Loews, Hyatt Centric.
scams.location: Online — Airbnb listings for Center City, Old City, Rittenhouse Square; Facebook Marketplace short-term rentals; off-platform booking referrals
scams.tldr: Fraudulent Airbnb and Facebook Marketplace listings advertise Center City or Old City apartments at 25–40% below hotel rates, then the "host" demands a Zelle or Venmo deposit before confirming — and either the apartment doesn't exist or the host cancels and keeps the off-platform money. Some also harvest your ID and credit-card photos for identity theft.
